rules.plain_language_rule: Power is the ability to produce high levels of force rapidly.
Power is determined by the interaction between force and movement velocity.
Many rugby actions have very short force-production windows, making rapid force production critical.
Power contributes to sprinting, acceleration, cutting, jumping, tackling, lifting, hand-offs, and other explosive rugby actions.
Strength and power must be profiled separately; high maximal strength does not guarantee high power.
Lower-body power characteristics can distinguish higher- from lower-level rugby players.
Power assessment should consider both absolute and relative outputs where appropriate.
The system should track power longitudinally alongside strength, body mass, and speed.
Training should eventually distinguish whether an athlete’s power limitation is primarily force-related, velocity-related, or mixed.
Speed is a critical rugby physical quality with clear transfer to attacking and defensive performance.
Speed should be divided into acceleration ability and maximal running speed rather than treated as one single quality.
Short sprint splits such as 10 m and 20 m can provide useful information about acceleration.
Longer sprint distances or flying-speed measures can provide information about maximal-speed ability.
Sprint split times should be stored because identical total sprint times can hide different speed profiles.
Faster sprint ability is associated with important rugby actions including line breaks, metres gained, defenders beaten, tries, defensive positioning, and tackle success.
Speed can differentiate playing standards, including high levels of rugby performance.
Speed development should be included in long-term rugby physical preparation rather than being treated as an optional extra.
Speed development should be interpreted alongside strength, power, body composition, and sprint mechanics.
Speed prescriptions should ultimately distinguish whether the athlete primarily needs acceleration development, maximal-speed development, or both.
Rugby requires sufficient aerobic endurance to sustain effective involvement over an 80-minute intermittent collision game.
Aerobic fitness supports movement around the field and recovery between high-intensity efforts.
Rugby endurance should not be represented solely as continuous running capacity.
Repeated sprint ability represents the capacity to reproduce high-intensity sprint efforts with limited performance decline.
Rugby requires repeated high-intensity effort ability beyond sprinting because contact actions also impose substantial metabolic demands.
Endurance assessment should consider the athlete’s ability to recover and reproduce performance, not merely their best single effort.
Performance decrement across repeated efforts can provide useful diagnostic information.
Aerobic fitness and repeated high-intensity ability can influence technical and tactical match performance under fatigue.
Endurance demands vary by rugby format, position, and playing level.
Sevens and 15-a-side rugby should not automatically share identical endurance benchmarks or conditioning prescriptions.
Endurance development should be integrated with speed, strength, power, and rugby-specific activities rather than viewed in isolation.
